title: I run 13 paper trading bots on one EC2 instance under systemd. Sharing the infrastructure, the risk engine, and the bugs that bit me
author: Inevitable_Ad2727
selftext:
What I've been doing is setting up a paper trading system to test as a form of statistics/experimentation. Most posts on this sub and similar will focus on trading strategies; however, I believe the majority of home systems fail due to the "boring" operational tasks.



The setup: 13 different trading strategies (mean reversion, trend with a regime-gated A/B clone, credit spreads, gap fade, defensive rotation, a passive SPY benchmark, and others) – each running independently as its own systemd service with its own Alpaca paper trading account, its own Discord channel, memory limits, and logrotate. There's also another independent risk management process that logs all of the daily account equities for all of the individual strategies at night and enforces kill lines that will shut down each strategy if they hit a certain number.



There's also a nightly cron job that takes all of the historical fill information from all of the different strategies and matches them together on a per ticker basis to build out a historical Profit & Loss (P/L) for each ticker. This is used to update the Excel spreadsheet that contains the overall metrics for the system.



I have learned some things the hard way (the detailed documentation for these experiences can be found in the "lessons-learned.md" document located within the repository):



\- Alpaca's bars API returns data oldest first. When using the start parameter set to today and a small limit, my bot would trade on close prices that were several hours old — and it only showed itself to me on days when there were large volumes traded. Therefore, it seemed like intermittent behavior.



\- A .save file was left in /etc/logrotate.d/ that caused log rotation to stop functioning on the entire fleet for over a week without showing any obvious signs of issues. Even though I had no alerts indicating there was something wrong with my infrastructure — always audit your infrastructure.



\- When editing .env files on Windows, CRLF line endings damaged webhook URLs and API keys without anyone noticing. sed -i 's/\\r$//' became a required part of my deployment script.



\- My option bot did not consider that being accepted does not equal opening a position. Until I redesigned the bot as a state machine that could only transition upon receipt of confirmation that the trade was filled, the bot's internal state kept drifting from reality.



\- Although I created two "identical" A/B clones of the same bot, they were not truly identical. They had different timing because the scanning loops were starting at slightly offset times. Timing matters.



Intentional Design Choices:



\- Every version of every strategy variant is different than its control group only by one mechanism.



\- The passive SPY benchmark trades with the same amount of capital so I'm measuring every single strategy versus doing nothing.



\- No profit or loss claims anywhere — intentionally: statistically speaking, weeks' worth of real-time data is basically noise.



Regarding AI: Because I want to be completely open, everything prior to this point I developed myself, the original bot, the first service file, etc., as well as the basic patterns. After that (creating new bot clones based on existing bots, creating new service files for those clones, etc.), as well as a great deal of my debugging was done using AI. All of the architecture and design decisions regarding this project are mine, and I am capable of defending any line of it.



Here is a link to the github page with the six most distinct bots, allocator, regime calculator, analytics pipeline, systemd units, etc., as well as the complete lessons-learned document: [https://github.com/Davin-Willis/trading-fleet-infrastructure](https://github.com/Davin-Willis/trading-fleet-infrastructure)



Happy to answer any questions you all have!

comments.author: No-Abbreviations1973
comments.body: did you ask it to make no mistake?

comments.author: Vast-Slice-1999
comments.body: did any strategy get killed by your risk manager during paper trading because of an infrastructure bug rather than market behavior?

replies.author: Inevitable_Ad2727
replies.body: Negative. I have a trend strategy bot that was my closest,  but that was genuinely just market behavior. I will say that I did have infrastructure bugs like stale market data and a state machine gap but none that got killed by my risk manager. As I scaled up to 13 bots, I realized that I wanted something watching account equity independently of what the bots believe about themselves.

comments.author: Tasty-Success-9268
comments.body: So is it a paid trading group or a paid course ?

replies.author: Inevitable_Ad2727
replies.body: Definitely not. I've just compiled my journey with algo/ai trading into a GitHub repository for anyone who may want to build something similar. I intentionally left out P/L to deter anyone from thinking this is a promotion of some kind.

comments.author: bartekrutkowski
comments.body:
The equity process protects against strategy state problems but it still shares the EC2, systemd, cron and network failure space and it can all go down in one unlucky event.

I would add two signals outside the host: an expected completion deadline for the nightly P&L pipeline and a periodic fleet level heartbeat. That catches both individual failures like the logrotate incident and the harder case where the host or scheduler disappears before it can send an alert.

replies.author: Inevitable_Ad2727
replies.body: That's genuinely something that never crossed my mind. I appreciate the advice!

comments.author: engineering-AF7
comments.body:
Solid work here. Have you considered building an app where you can control it all?   
  
I deployed alphaflowseven (my testbench) using Railway, and I really love my workflow now. I use Claude Code in  Visual Studio, as soon as I commit to Github, Railway picks it up and deploys (to a dev instance)

replies.author: Inevitable_Ad2727
replies.body:
Thanks! I was very intentional about not building a control app. The read side of the control plane is already working well in that each bot posts trades & errors into their respective Discord channels; a risk manager posts a daily fleet summary, which allows me to view all of this on my phone. If/when I need write control, the next layer of my implementation will be a Discord bot with two simple commands (pause-bot/show-positions), so there's one less service to deploy and maintain.  
I like your railway deployment workflow though and plan to implement it into any future projects -- seems very clean.

replies.author: engineering-AF7
replies.body: Cool, the control app for sure adds work. The decision makes sense.

comments.author: hikewithcaramel
comments.body:
This is the first post I've seen on here that actually reads like my own experience, and I've been deep in the weeds on this for 6+ months (two paper-trading systems, spread-betting bots + a horse racing value model, built entirely through AI collaboration since I don't code myself).
The "boring operational tasks" line is exactly right — nearly every real bug I've found has been infrastructure, not strategy. Had a bot silently never call its own decision engine at all for weeks (import failure swallowed silently, same category as your logrotate .save file), a P&L formula quietly breaking risk controls, state drifting after restarts. None of it showed up until I went looking for evidence rather than trusting "should be working."
Also respect the no-profit-claims-yet stance — same rule here. Data-gated, not calendar-gated, and short samples don't mean anything yet.
Question if you don't mind: how are you handling comparing strategies fairly when market conditions shift mid-test? I've been wrestling with whether X trades on one instrument over a few weeks is really an independent sample of anything, given regime overlap between concurrent strategies.

replies.author: Inevitable_Ad2727
replies.body:
I'll provide you with my approach to both issues, although neither has been totally resolved.

Regime shifts during testing: the easiest method I've used is a benchmark bot. All tests are compared over the same time frame against a buy & hold SPY strategy. So if the regime shifts during testing, it shifts for the benchmark bot too. Instead of asking "was your strategy profitable?" I'm asking "did it beat doing nothing in the same environment?" This provides slightly better control over regime than absolute returns, but I still don't believe I've adequately addressed the problem. One strategy may outperform the benchmark in one regime and lose money in another. Given that many of our test windows are only two weeks long, we're best-case sampling one regime per test.

Independence issue: I believe you're correct here, and it's the area I'm by far least comfortable with. Most of the concurrent strategies trading the same asset class are trading within the same regime. Consequently there isn't independence when each strategy moves the same direction in a single week. At best that's one regime sample, not N. I eventually stopped looking at "15 bots" as 15 individual experiments and began seeing it as one experiment viewed from 15 different vantage points. While this makes the fleet very good for finding infrastructure errors (these are independent, a state-drift error in one bot tells me nothing about regime), it greatly diminishes the fleet's capability to determine if any strategy has an edge.

What continues to go through my mind is that short concurrent samples can easily demonstrate a strategy is broken (fails against the benchmark under all conditions), but they can hardly prove or disprove whether a strategy has any edge. I recently backtested the entire fleet and the results were completely congruent with what I'd expect based on the above. There was essentially no correlation between the live leaderboard and the 5-year backtest characteristics. That's precisely what would happen if a few weeks of concurrently running live data is essentially just noise. So I've come to accept that the primary function of the fleet is finding bugs and enforcing process discipline, and only secondarily identifying edges.

Curious how you handle regime shift on the horse-racing model, since you could potentially have more independent samples than instrument trading allows.
